The lighthouse keeper had not seen another soul in forty-three days, not since the supply boat missed its summer run. He kept the lamp burning anyway, polishing the great lens each evening and trimming the wick with the same brass scissors his grandfather had used. On the forty-fourth night a ship veered toward the reef without its lights, and only the keeper's steady beam kept it off the rocks. The captain rowed ashore and pressed a coin into the keeper's hand, a coin older than either of them, stamped with a harbor that had vanished from every chart. The keeper turned it over in the lamplight, then handed it back. He had been saving for nothing in particular, he realized, and the light was not for sale.
